Nutrient mobility decides which leaf to look at: mobile nutrients such as nitrogen, potassium, phosphorus and magnesium show symptoms on the old leaves first, because the plant relocates them to the new ones; immobile nutrients such as calcium and boron show symptoms on the new leaves and at the growing point.

Some visual patterns in rice serve as a reference: necrosis in an inverted V shape, running from the tip down the margins of an old leaf, points to potassium; very narrow, erect new leaves with a bronzed or purple tint at the tips point to phosphorus; a whole field yellowing at tillering and panicle initiation points to nitrogen; and a deficiency that appears in patches rather than across the whole area is a typical potassium pattern. Herbicide toxicity imitates deficiency, but it appears immediately after spraying — that temporal proximity is what separates the two cases. Finally, grain and silage are not the same crop from the soil's point of view: phosphorus is almost entirely translocated to the grain, followed by nitrogen, while potassium and calcium remain mostly in the straw, so in silage, which also removes the vegetative part, fertility problems appear earlier.
checklist: Do not wait for a symptom: by the time it shows, the loss has already happened.
Mobile nutrients show on old leaves; immobile ones on new leaves.
Diagnose from a soil test and field history, never from a leaf photo alone.
Damage appearing right after spraying is herbicide, not deficiency.
Do not use a grain recommendation for a crop destined for silage.

advice: The decision here is made by counting, not by calendar, and this group has the cheapest standardised sampling of all. The logic rests on three thresholds: the equilibrium level, the economic damage level and the control level, which sits just below it. For corn soil pests, use a soil sample thirty by thirty centimetres and fifteen deep, sieved — for wireworm, two or more insects per sample already call for control, and an average of one per sample already causes significant damage. For fall armyworm, sample the number of attacked plants at five random points within one hectare: in fields with a potential of at least a hundred bags, 10% of plants showing early symptoms already indicates a need for control, and the most sensitive stage is eight to ten leaves. The first sign is larvae scraping the leaves and leaving transparent windows.

In soybean, the beat cloth is the method: a preferably white cloth, one metre long, stretched between two rows; shake one row vigorously over it and count adults and juveniles, weekly during the critical period. The minimum is six samples up to ten hectares, eight up to thirty and ten up to a hundred, dividing larger areas into hundred-hectare blocks. Sample soil pests before planting, because measures taken after the crop is established are inefficient. Count the nymphs alongside the adults: third to fifth instar stink bugs cause similar damage and make up most of the population in the reproductive period, with an action threshold of two stink bugs per metre of row for grain and one for seed. Sample during the cooler parts of the day, because stink bugs are quick and escape in the heat. This has a measured return: across 196 reference units in Paraná in the 2017/2018 season, integrated pest management cut insecticide applications by more than 43% while keeping yield equivalent. Choose the product by selectivity to natural enemies as well as by cost and toxicity, always follow current MAPA registrations, and treat seed only where there is a history of the problem, never as blind routine.
checklist: Count before spraying: the decision is by threshold, not by calendar.
Corn: 10% of plants with scraped leaves already calls for control.
Soybean: a minimum of ten beat-cloth samples up to a hundred hectares.
Sample soil pests before planting.
Count nymphs alongside adults, and sample in the cooler hours of the day.

advice: Here water is fine management, not watering when you remember: there is a soil tension limit measured in kPa, and it differs by irrigation system. In eggplant, you irrigate when the tensiometer reads 30 to 50 kPa under sprinkler or furrow, or 10 to 15 kPa under drip, using the lower end of the range at the most critical stages, in sandy soils and under high evaporative demand. The sensor goes at 50% of the effective root depth and ten to twenty centimetres from the plant, effective depth being where about 80% of the roots are concentrated.

Excess water is as damaging as shortage: it drives excessive plant growth, hinders flowering and fruit set, favours soil diseases through inadequate aeration and leaches nutrients. Shortage weighs most at flowering and fruiting, causing flowers and fruit to abort, reducing fruit growth and producing quality defects — misshapen and uneven fruit, blossom-end rot and bitter flavour. Leaf wilting at the end of the morning is a rough but useful sign that irrigation is overdue. And the choice of system is a plant-health decision, not just a hydraulic one: furrow and drip reduce foliar disease because they do not wet the foliage, but against the tomato leafminer sprinkler is an advantage, because it knocks down eggs, larvae and pupae. The decision depends on the problem that dominates your area.
checklist: Use a different tension limit for drip than for sprinkler or furrow.
Install the sensor at 50% of effective root depth and ten to twenty centimetres from the plant.
Do not let water run short during flowering and fruiting.
Wilting at the end of the morning indicates overdue irrigation.
Choose the irrigation system according to the problem that dominates your area.

advice: Excess nutrient has symptoms of its own and unbalances the others. In onion, excess nitrogen produces thick-necked plants, raises susceptibility to foliar disease and shortens post-harvest storage life; excess potassium induces magnesium and calcium deficiency; excess phosphorus induces zinc and copper deficiency. That is why correcting one nutrient without looking at the others usually creates the next problem.

Mobility tells you which leaf to inspect: nitrogen, potassium, phosphorus and magnesium appear first on the old leaves, while calcium and sulfur appear on the new ones — a new onion leaf falling over without breaking is the calcium signature. Two textures are worth memorising: necrosis that appears abruptly, with no preceding chlorosis, points to zinc, copper or manganese; necrosis with a velvety texture is the characteristic mark of iron, distinct from all the others. In Brazilian soils under normal conditions, only boron and zinc and, in some cases, copper tend to be short for onion. And watch for the false positive: low temperatures, excess water or prolonged drought can produce symptoms very similar to nitrogen deficiency.
checklist: Do not correct one nutrient without looking at the ones it unbalances.
Old leaves first: nitrogen, potassium, phosphorus, magnesium. New leaves: calcium, sulfur.
Abrupt necrosis with no preceding chlorosis suggests zinc, copper or manganese.
Necrosis with a velvety texture is the mark of iron.
Cold, waterlogging and drought all imitate nitrogen deficiency.

advice: Management here is cultural and collective before it is chemical. At field level: adopt crop rotation, destroy crop residues immediately after harvest, keep the area free of weeds and other host plants for insects and mites, and use cultivars adapted to the region. At the collective level — and this is what makes the group different — growers have to act together: concentrate planting within each micro-region into the shortest possible window, use inputs in a coordinated way so common problems are faced by everyone at the same time, and systematically disinfest crates and transport to reduce the spread of pests between regions. Inspect regularly, with special attention to field edges and to the weediest spots, because that is where infestation concentrates.

The greatest pest damage in this group is usually indirect, through virus. Whitefly has been known in Brazil since 1923 and was found on tomato and cabbage in 1993, associated with geminivirus symptoms, with severe outbreaks and losses of up to 50% of production: adults and nymphs inject a sugary substance and a toxin that leave the internal walls of the fruit whitish and spongy and encourage sooty mould. Timing also governs: against the small borer, spraying must begin from flowering, with the jet directed at the flower buds and fruit, because by the time you see a hole in the fruit the larva is already inside. And one editorial safety rule: do not copy an active ingredient or a dose from any source, because pesticide registrations change every season — consult the current MAPA register.
checklist: Destroy crop residues immediately after harvest.
Concentrate the micro-region's planting into the smallest possible window.
Disinfest crates and vehicles between areas.
Inspect the field edges, not only the middle.
Start spraying at flowering, not when you see a hole in the fruit.
